item.title: Shop below, flats above: what lenders make of mixed-use
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

In recent years, residential property investors have navigated a challenging landscape marked by tax adjustments, rental reforms, and rising borrowing costs. Amidst these changes, some are turning their attention to a less conventional investment opportunity: mixed-use properties, particularly those combining a shop on the ground floor with flats above. While these properties can offer dual income streams from a single asset, they also present unique challenges when it comes to securing financing.

What Are Mixed-Use Properties?

Mixed-use properties are buildings that serve both residential and commercial purposes. A common example is a high street shop with residential flats above. These properties can be appealing to investors seeking diversification, as they generate rental income from both tenants and business occupiers. However, their hybrid nature means they fall into a distinct category when it comes to mortgages, often requiring specialised lending solutions.

Challenges with Mortgage Applications

Securing a mortgage for a mixed-use property can be more complex than obtaining financing for a purely residential or commercial property. Many high street lenders are hesitant to finance these assets due to their dual-purpose nature, which can make them harder to value and sell if the borrower defaults. Additionally, lenders may perceive mixed-use properties as higher risk, particularly if the commercial element relies on a specific tenant or business type.

For investors considering this route, it could be worth exploring specialist lenders or mortgage brokers who have experience with mixed-use properties. These professionals may offer more tailored solutions and a deeper understanding of the unique risks and rewards associated with such investments.

Benefits of Mixed-Use Investments

Despite the challenges, mixed-use properties can offer several advantages. The combination of residential and commercial tenants can provide a steady income stream, potentially reducing reliance on a single source of rental revenue. Furthermore, these properties often benefit from prime high street locations, which can enhance their long-term value and appeal.

For those willing to navigate the complexities of financing and management, mixed-use properties could represent a strategic addition to a diversified property portfolio. However, thorough due diligence is essential, particularly in assessing the viability of the commercial element and understanding the specific lending criteria for these assets.

As with any property investment, seeking professional advice and carefully evaluating the risks and rewards can help ensure a sound decision. Mixed-use properties may not be suitable for everyone, but for the right investor, they could unlock unique opportunities in the UK property market.

item.title: The Overlooked Repairs That Become an Investor’s Most Expensive Problems
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Many buy-to-let landlords discover too late that small maintenance issues can snowball into costly repairs if left unattended. What begins as a minor leak or superficial crack often develops into structural damage requiring extensive work - potentially disrupting tenancies and eroding rental yields significantly.

Common Minor Issues That Escalate

Property investors might be surprised how seemingly trivial problems can become serious over time. Some frequently overlooked concerns include:

  • Dripping taps or small water leaks that gradually damage flooring and subfloor structures
  • Worn window seals allowing moisture penetration and potential timber rot
  • Minor cracks in walls or ceilings that may indicate foundation movement
  • Sticking doors or windows suggesting frame warping or subsidence
  • Guttering blockages leading to water ingress and exterior deterioration

Why Preventative Maintenance Pays Off

Whilst immediate repairs might appear an unnecessary expense, proactive maintenance typically proves far more economical than emergency fixes. Landlords may wish to consider:

  • Scheduling biannual property inspections between tenancies
  • Budgeting 1-2% of the property value annually for maintenance
  • Promptly addressing tenant reports of minor issues
  • Building relationships with reliable local tradespeople
  • Keeping detailed records of all works completed

A stitch in time doesn't just save nine in property maintenance - it could potentially save thousands of pounds in avoidable damage whilst maintaining the asset value and rental potential. Savvy investors recognise that proactive care forms part of responsible portfolio management.

item.title: ‘Christmas comes early’ for housebuilders as shares surge on buyer scheme
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK government’s announcement of a new first-time buyer scheme has sparked a significant surge in housebuilder shares, offering a potential boost to the property market. Named ‘Your First Home’, the initiative aims to help eligible buyers in England purchase new-build properties with deposits as low as 2.5%. The scheme includes a government-backed equity loan of up to 20% of the property’s value, alongside an initial interest-free period. Full details, including income limits and local price caps, are expected to be unveiled at next month’s Budget.

How the Scheme Could Impact Housebuilders

The proposed scheme has already had a positive effect on the stock market, with shares in major housebuilders rising sharply. Companies such as Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, and Taylor Wimpey saw gains of around 12-15%, whilst Crest Nicholson and Vistry also experienced notable increases. Building materials firms, including Ibstock and Marshalls, joined the rally, with their shares climbing by 21% and 12% respectively.

Analysts suggest that developers with a strong focus on open-market sales, particularly in the south and south-east of England, are likely to benefit the most from the initiative. Conversely, firms with less exposure to these markets or properties priced above the scheme’s proposed caps may see relatively slower growth. Anthony Codling, managing director at RBC Capital Markets, described the announcement as a “big catalyst” for the sector, noting that it has effectively brought “Christmas early” for UK housebuilders.

Potential Benefits for First-Time Buyers

The primary goal of ‘Your First Home’ is to reduce the deposit barrier faced by first-time buyers, making homeownership more accessible. By offering a 20% equity loan and an initial interest-free period, the scheme could significantly lower upfront costs. This approach mirrors elements of the former Help to Buy equity loan programme, though final terms are yet to be confirmed.

The introduction of income limits and local property price caps is expected to ensure that the scheme targets those who need it most. For buyers, this could mean greater affordability in areas where property prices have historically been prohibitive. Additionally, the focus on new-build homes may help stimulate demand in this sector, supporting both buyers and developers.

Market Reaction and Future Outlook

The announcement comes at a time when housebuilders are grappling with weaker buyer confidence and rising construction costs. The potential boost from ‘Your First Home’ could provide much-needed relief, particularly for firms heavily reliant on new-build sales. Investors appear optimistic, with the sharp rise in housebuilder shares reflecting confidence in the scheme’s potential to rejuvenate the market.

Whilst further details, including implementation timelines and costs, are expected in the Budget, the initial response suggests that the initiative could be a game-changer for both buyers and the property sector. Borrowers considering their options may wish to keep an eye on developments as the scheme takes shape.

As the government prepares to finalise the details of ‘Your First Home’, the property market awaits what could be a transformative initiative for first-time buyers and housebuilders alike. With the Budget just weeks away, stakeholders are keen to see how the scheme will be rolled out and what it could mean for the future of homeownership in the UK.

item.title: Landlord exodus: More than 500 rental homes leaving PRS every day
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent analysis by property data firm TwentyEA reveals a significant trend in the UK’s private rented sector (PRS), with an estimated 505 rental homes exiting the market daily in 2026. This marks a sharp increase compared to 2020, where the rate was less than a third of current levels. The findings highlight ongoing challenges for landlords, driven by a combination of regulatory changes, taxation pressures, and rising costs.

The Impact of Regulatory Reforms

The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in England on 1 May, has introduced sweeping changes to the rental landscape. Key reforms include the abolition of Section 21 evictions, the introduction of a new tenancy system, and restrictions on rental bidding. Whilst these measures aim to improve tenant protections, they have coincided with a surge in landlord sales. In 2024, around 111,696 rental properties left the PRS, a figure that rose to approximately 181,000 in 2025. Although there were initial signs of a slowdown in landlord exits earlier this year, the trend appears to have regained momentum.

It’s worth noting that TwentyEA’s analysis does not directly attribute the rise in landlord sales to the Renters’ Rights Act. Instead, the firm points to broader pressures on landlord returns, including taxation, mortgage costs, and upcoming energy-efficiency requirements. These factors, combined with regulatory changes, have created a challenging environment for property investors.

Future Challenges for Landlords

Looking ahead, landlords face further regulatory and financial hurdles. From late 2026, the government plans to introduce a mandatory PRS Database, requiring landlords to register and pay an annual fee. Additionally, the introduction of a Landlord Ombudsman is expected in 2028, adding another layer of oversight. Tax changes are also on the horizon, with separate property income tax rates of 22%, 42%, and 47% set to take effect from April 2027.

Energy-efficiency standards present another significant cost for landlords. By 1 October 2030, privately rented homes must meet higher standards, unless exemptions apply. Estimates suggest landlords may need to spend up to £10,000 per property on qualifying improvements, with average costs projected at £5,400 for properties below the required standard. For owners of high-value rental properties in England, the proposed High Value Council Tax Surcharge could add further financial strain from April 2028.

The National Picture

TwentyEA’s data indicates that the PRS has lost 18.6% of its rental stock nationally since the start of the decade. In London, the figure stands at 14.2%. Whilst the capital has seen a slightly lower rate of decline compared to the national average, the overall trend underscores the growing pressures on the rental market. With regulatory and financial challenges continuing to mount, landlords may increasingly consider selling their properties, potentially reducing the availability of rental homes for tenants.

As the PRS evolves, both landlords and tenants face a changing landscape. For landlords, staying informed about forthcoming regulations and planning for potential costs could help navigate these challenges. Meanwhile, tenants may find themselves with fewer rental options, highlighting the need for balanced policies that support both parties in the UK’s housing market.

item.title: Property fall-throughs jump as cost of failed sales climbs
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent data reveals a concerning trend in the UK property market, with a notable rise in the number of property transactions falling through before completion. According to analysis by House Buyer Bureau, using data from TwentyCi, an estimated 71,959 sales collapsed in the second quarter of 2026. This marks a 6.6% increase compared to the previous quarter, highlighting ongoing challenges in the homebuying process. Whilst the figures remain lower than those recorded in the same period last year, the rise underscores the financial and emotional toll that failed transactions can have on buyers, sellers, and estate agents alike.

The Financial Impact of Fall-Throughs

Failed property transactions come with significant financial consequences. House Buyer Bureau estimates that fall-throughs cost buyers and sellers £257.9 million during the quarter, up from £239.7 million in the first three months of 2026. This £18 million increase reflects the growing financial burden associated with collapsed sales. The average cost of a failed transaction also rose to £3,584, representing a 0.9% increase from the previous quarter and a 2.8% rise compared to the same period in 2025.

For estate agents, the impact extends beyond the immediate loss of potential commission. A fall-through often means remarketing the property, restarting negotiations, and rebuilding broken chains, all of which can be time-consuming and uncertain. Traditional agents, who typically receive their fees upon completion, may face delayed or lost income, adding to the challenges of managing such scenarios.

The Broader Implications for Buyers and Sellers

For homeowners and buyers, a collapsed sale can be particularly stressful. Sellers may face wasted time, additional costs, and the uncertainty of having to relist their property. This can be especially disruptive if they have already made plans based on the assumption that their sale would complete. Buyers, too, may experience financial losses and the frustration of needing to restart their property search.

Chris Hodgkinson, Managing Director of House Buyer Bureau, commented on the findings: “Whilst the number of fall-throughs remains lower than last year’s levels, the latest increase highlights the fragility of the homebuying process. The rising average cost of failed transactions means that every collapse carries significant financial consequences for those involved.”

Despite the challenges, there is some positive news. The overall volume of fall-throughs is still below last year’s figures, suggesting that there may be opportunities to improve certainty in the transaction process. Hodgkinson added: “There is considerable scope to enhance the reliability of property transactions, which would benefit buyers, sellers, and agents alike.”

As the property market continues to navigate these complexities, homeowners may wish to explore ways to minimise the risk of fall-throughs, such as seeking professional advice and ensuring thorough preparation before entering the buying or selling process.

item.title: New student-living operator launches
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

A new player has entered the UK's purpose-built student accommodation sector with the launch of Residium, a student housing operator based in Coventry. The company aims to collaborate with both property owners and academic institutions to expand its portfolio of student living spaces across key university cities.

Expanding Student Housing Options

Residium's arrival comes at a time when demand for quality student accommodation continues to grow across Britain. The company specialises in developing and managing purpose-built student housing, with plans to establish partnerships with universities and private landlords. This model could provide fresh opportunities for property investors looking to enter the student rental market.

Students and property owners alike may benefit from Residium's professional management approach. The operator focuses on creating modern living spaces tailored to student needs, which could help landlords maintain high occupancy rates whilst ensuring tenants enjoy comfortable, well-maintained accommodation.

The Student Accommodation Market

The UK's student housing sector has shown remarkable resilience in recent years, with demand consistently outstripping supply in many university towns. Purpose-built student accommodation often commands premium rents compared to traditional buy-to-let properties, making it an attractive proposition for investors.

Residium's Coventry base positions it well to serve one of England's fastest-growing student populations. The city's two universities host over 50,000 students, many of whom struggle to find suitable housing. Similar pressures exist in other university towns, suggesting potential for expansion beyond the Midlands.

For landlords considering student rentals, partnering with an established operator like Residium could offer several advantages. Professional management typically handles everything from maintenance to rent collection, potentially reducing void periods and tenant disputes. However, investors should carefully research any management agreement's terms before committing.

As the academic year begins, Residium's launch highlights the ongoing importance of quality student housing solutions. The company's success may depend on its ability to form strong local partnerships whilst delivering accommodation that meets both student expectations and investor requirements.

item.title: BTR delivers 61% of new homes in regeneration areas
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals that Build-to-Rent (BTR) developments now account for nearly two-thirds of new housing in UK regeneration zones. With 61% of recently completed homes in these areas falling under the BTR sector, the figures highlight its growing influence on urban renewal and local economies.

BTR's role in housing delivery and regeneration

The latest industry analysis shows BTR schemes are becoming central to housing supply in regeneration hotspots across Britain. These purpose-built rental developments are particularly prevalent in former industrial areas and underutilised urban districts undergoing transformation.

Key findings indicate that BTR projects are delivering more than just housing stock. They're acting as catalysts for wider regeneration by attracting new amenities, creating employment opportunities and boosting local services. The model appears particularly effective at:

  • Accelerating construction timelines through institutional investment
  • Introducing higher density housing in well-connected locations
  • Supporting population growth in previously declining areas

Impact on local communities and demand

The concentration of BTR properties in regeneration zones correlates with noticeable demographic shifts. Many developments report attracting younger professionals and key workers who value the combination of modern facilities and transport links often featured in these schemes.

Housing experts suggest this trend could reshape local housing markets by:

  • Increasing rental stock quality in areas with historically poor private rented sector options
  • Stimulating demand for supporting businesses like cafés, gyms and co-working spaces
  • Potentially easing pressure on traditional buy-to-let markets in surrounding neighbourhoods

While the growth of BTR in regeneration areas shows no signs of slowing, some commentators note the importance of ensuring these developments maintain mixed communities and affordability. Local authorities increasingly include requirements for affordable rental components within BTR planning approvals.

The research underscores how institutional investment in rental housing is transforming Britain's urban landscapes, particularly in areas earmarked for renewal. As the sector matures, its role in meeting housing needs while supporting wider regeneration objectives appears set to expand further.

item.title: Landbay announces new tracker options for landlords
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Specialist buy-to-let lender Landbay has expanded its product range with 11 new tracker mortgages aimed at property investors, alongside rate reductions and adjusted affordability criteria on selected refinancing deals. The move comes as the lender seeks to strengthen its position in the competitive landlord mortgage market.

New tracker mortgage options for landlords

Landlords now have more choice with Landbay's latest tracker mortgage additions, which include options at 60%, 65% and 75% loan-to-value (LTV) ratios. These tracker products follow the Bank of England base rate plus a fixed margin, offering landlords potential savings when interest rates fall while providing transparency in pricing.

The lender has also reduced rates across several products in its range, with cuts of up to 0.15 percentage points on selected fixed-rate deals. These adjustments reflect current market conditions and may make Landbay's products more attractive to property investors reviewing their mortgage options.

Refinancing criteria adjustments

For landlords looking to refinance, Landbay has made changes to its affordability testing on certain products. The lender has reduced its interest coverage ratio (ICR) stress test from 145% to 140% at 75% LTV for limited company applications, potentially making it easier for some portfolio landlords to secure financing.

Other key features of the enhanced product range include:

  • No minimum income requirement for personal applications
  • Products available for both personal and limited company borrowers
  • Free valuations included on all products
  • No fees for product transfers

Mortgage brokers specialising in buy-to-let may find these changes particularly noteworthy when advising landlord clients. The expanded tracker options could appeal to investors who prefer the flexibility of variable-rate mortgages, especially those anticipating potential base rate movements in the coming months.

As with any financial product, landlords might consider seeking professional advice to determine whether these new options suit their individual circumstances and investment strategy. The property market remains competitive, with lenders continually adjusting their offerings to attract business from professional landlords and property investors.

item.title: Mallorca and Italy prime continue to shine
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Over recent years, Mallorca and Italy have emerged as hotspots for international property buyers, with prime markets in both destinations showing robust growth. According to recent trends, these locations are attracting heightened interest from investors and holiday homebuyers alike, driven by their combination of lifestyle appeal and strong property market performance.

Mallorca’s Allure for Property Buyers

Mallorca, the largest of Spain’s Balearic Islands, continues to captivate buyers with its stunning landscapes, Mediterranean climate, and luxury property offerings. The island’s prime real estate market has seen steady price increases, supported by high demand from international purchasers. British buyers, in particular, are drawn to Mallorca’s blend of natural beauty and accessibility, with direct flights from the UK making it a convenient second-home destination.

Luxury villas and coastal properties remain the most sought-after, often featuring private pools, sea views, and proximity to exclusive amenities. The island’s appeal is further enhanced by its thriving cultural scene, world-class gastronomy, and outdoor activities, making it a year-round destination for those seeking both relaxation and adventure.

Italy’s Prime Property Market Strengthens

Italy, known for its rich history, picturesque countryside, and architectural charm, is also experiencing a surge in prime property transactions. Regions such as Tuscany, Umbria, and the Amalfi Coast are particularly popular, offering a mix of historic villas, farmhouses, and luxury apartments. These properties often appeal to buyers looking for a blend of heritage and modern comforts, with many opting to restore traditional homes to their former glory.

The Italian property market benefits from its diverse offerings, catering to a wide range of tastes and budgets. From rustic countryside retreats to elegant urban residences, Italy’s prime market is thriving, bolstered by its reputation as a cultural and culinary haven. The country’s Golden Visa programme, which offers residency to non-EU investors, has also contributed to increased interest from international buyers.

Factors Driving Demand

Several factors are contributing to the growing appeal of Mallorca and Italy’s prime property markets. Lifestyle considerations play a significant role, with buyers prioritising locations that offer a high quality of life, scenic beauty, and cultural richness. Additionally, the stability and potential for capital appreciation in these markets make them attractive investment opportunities.

For British buyers, the favourable exchange rate and the possibility of securing residency through property investment further enhance the appeal. Both destinations also benefit from well-established infrastructure, including international schools, healthcare facilities, and transport links, making them practical choices for families and retirees.

As Mallorca and Italy continue to shine on the global property stage, their prime markets are likely to remain a focal point for international buyers. With their unique blend of lifestyle benefits and investment potential, these destinations offer compelling opportunities for those looking to purchase a second home or expand their property portfolio.

item.title: What Makes a New Development Worth a Closer Look for Investors?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New developments often dazzle potential buyers with glossy brochures showcasing sleek interiors and state-of-the-art amenities. For property investors, however, assessing whether a development holds genuine investment potential involves looking beyond the surface appeal. Location, demographic trends and long-term growth prospects all play crucial roles in determining if a new build could deliver solid returns.

Key Factors Influencing a Development's Investment Potential

Whilst attractive specifications may catch the eye, savvy investors typically consider several fundamental aspects before committing to a new development. These include:

  • Location fundamentals: Proximity to transport links, schools and employment hubs often drives demand. Established areas with regeneration plans may offer balanced risk and reward.
  • Local rental demand: Developments in areas with strong tenant demand—particularly near universities or business districts—could provide steady rental income.
  • Developer track record: Reputable developers with a history of delivering quality projects on time may reduce potential risks.
  • Future infrastructure: Planned transport improvements or commercial developments in the area might enhance long-term capital growth.

Understanding the Local Market Dynamics

Beyond the bricks and mortar, investors might wish to research the surrounding area thoroughly. Demographic shifts such as an influx of young professionals or growing families could indicate rising demand for certain property types. Examining local price trends, void periods and rental yields compared to regional averages may provide valuable insights.

Investors could also consider how the development fits within the wider local property landscape. Premium-priced units in an area dominated by affordable housing might struggle to achieve expected returns, whilst competitively priced properties in undersupplied markets could present opportunities.

Balancing Short-Term Appeal with Long-Term Potential

New developments frequently offer incentives like stamp duty contributions or furniture packages, which can appear attractive initially. However, investors may find it beneficial to evaluate how the property might perform over a five to ten-year period. Factors such as maintenance costs, potential for value-added refurbishment and the development's ageing process should form part of the assessment.

Whilst new builds can provide modern living standards that appeal to tenants, some investors prefer properties with character in established areas. There is no universal right answer—each investment strategy depends on individual goals, risk appetite and timescales.

Property investment always carries risks alongside potential rewards. Investors might consider consulting independent financial advisers and conducting thorough due diligence before committing to any new development opportunity.

item.title: Industry warns of risks after government unveils 2.5% deposit scheme
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The government has revealed plans for a new equity loan scheme that could see first-time buyers purchase new-build properties with deposits as low as 2.5%. Dubbed 'Your First Home', the initiative combines small deposits with government-backed loans covering up to 20% of a property's value. While designed to help aspiring homeowners overcome deposit hurdles, some industry experts have raised concerns about potential market distortions.

How the new scheme could work

Under the proposed system, first-time buyers would secure a mortgage for 77.5% of the property value, supplemented by a 20% government equity loan and their 2.5% deposit. The government loan would initially be interest-free, potentially offering monthly savings compared to traditional 95% mortgages. The scheme will reportedly feature income limits and regional price caps, with full details expected in next month's Budget.

The initiative specifically targets new-build properties from participating developers, who will contribute towards scheme costs. This structure bears similarities to the previous Help to Buy programme, though crucial details about repayment terms, interest-free periods and eligibility criteria remain undisclosed.

Industry reaction and concerns

Property analysts have noted the scheme could provide timely support for both first-time buyers and housebuilders. Lucian Cook of Savills commented that the initiative comes at a "relatively depressed" point in the housing market cycle, potentially offering the government favourable investment returns if rates decline in coming years.

However, critics warn the policy could artificially inflate new-build prices, as seen with previous demand-side interventions. Some industry observers suggest such schemes risk creating dependency on government support rather than addressing fundamental supply issues in the housing market.

The government maintains the programme will complement existing planning reforms and boost housing delivery. With the private sector currently building below capacity, ministers hope the scheme will stimulate construction activity while helping buyers onto the property ladder.

As with any government-backed mortgage initiative, prospective buyers may wish to carefully compare all available options and seek independent financial advice before committing. The full implications of the scheme will become clearer when detailed terms are published in the forthcoming Budget announcement.

item.title: Landlords could still face fines for letting agent failures
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords in England are being reminded that hiring a letting agent does not necessarily absolve them of legal responsibilities under the recently implemented Renters' Rights Act. Despite delegating management tasks, property owners could still face substantial penalties if compliance failures occur – even when these result from agent errors.

Shared accountability under new regulations

Since 1 May 2024, stricter rental regulations have introduced fines reaching £7,000 for certain breaches, with persistent offenders potentially facing penalties up to £40,000. Government guidance clarifies that while landlords may employ agents to fulfil legal obligations, ultimate accountability often remains shared. Industry experts highlight that landlords cannot assume automatic protection from enforcement action simply by engaging a managing agent.

Paul Endacott of 1st Avenue notes: "When your appointed agent makes compliance errors, you might still bear responsibility for those failures. Many landlords don't realise they could face serious consequences for their agent's oversights." This shared liability structure means both parties must maintain rigorous standards across tenancy management, safety certifications, deposit protection and licensing requirements.

Evolving expectations for property management

The regulatory landscape has transformed what constitutes competent lettings management. Where landlords previously prioritised rental income and tenant placement speed, compliance documentation and audit trails now carry equal importance. "Property management has essentially become a compliance risk management role," Endacott observes.

Critical areas demanding meticulous record-keeping include:

  • Right to Rent verification documents
  • Deposit protection scheme paperwork
  • Electrical and gas safety certificates
  • Local authority licensing approvals

Enforcement authorities increasingly examine whether landlords and agents can demonstrate proper processes were followed, not just claim they were implemented. This evidentiary requirement raises the operational standard across the private rented sector.

Navigating variable liability arrangements

Responsibility allocation differs across regulatory areas. For Right to Rent checks, written agreements can explicitly transfer liability to agents. However, most other obligations maintain joint accountability. The Renters' Rights Act permits enforcement against landlords, agents, or both depending on where fault lies for specific breaches.

Property owners might consider:

  • Reviewing agent contracts for clear compliance responsibility clauses
  • Requesting regular compliance reporting from managing agents
  • Conducting periodic audits of essential documentation

As regulations continue evolving, proactive landlords are adapting their oversight approaches to mitigate risks in this more demanding operating environment. The key lies in understanding that delegation doesn't automatically mean discharging responsibility.

item.title: Renters face fiercest competition of 2026 as London demand jumps
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London's rental market saw its most competitive conditions of 2026 in August, with 24 prospective tenants vying for each available property according to Foxtons' latest data. The summer lettings season reached its peak intensity, though shifting patterns suggest the traditional August rush has become more evenly spread across July and August since the Renters' Rights Act (RRA) came into force.

Shifting seasonal patterns in London lettings

While August typically represents the annual high point for rental activity, Foxtons observed a 3% decline in tenant registrations between July and August this year. This suggests the market peak has broadened across both summer months since the RRA's introduction. Despite this change, the combined figures for July and August still represent the busiest period of 2026 so far.

The agency reported an average of 17.9 renters per property across the first eight months of 2026 - a figure that remains consistent with 2025 levels. Interestingly, August saw a 2.9% year-on-year increase in new rental listings, though supply dipped 5.2% compared with July's figures. Foxtons noted that every month in 2026 has seen more new listings than the corresponding period last year.

Regional variations across the capital

London's rental landscape shows significant geographical variations. Central London experienced the most dramatic supply contraction, with new instructions down 20% year-on-year, while North London saw a more modest 5% reduction. West London stood out as the only area where tenant registrations increased (up 5.2%), contrasting with significant declines elsewhere.

Rental budgets averaged £571 per week in August, representing a 1.9% decrease from July. Central London maintained its position as the most expensive area at £632 weekly, while West London saw budgets fall 2.2% below 2025 levels. One-bedroom flats recorded the strongest annual price growth among property types, with tenant budgets increasing by 3.4%.

Landlord activity persists despite regulatory changes

The data suggests many landlords continue operating in the capital despite the RRA's implementation. However, the year-to-date figures present a more nuanced picture - new instructions across London remain 13% below 2025 levels, while tenant registrations have fallen 12.3%. This supply-demand imbalance has created particularly fierce competition in some boroughs.

Prospective tenants in London might consider broadening their search criteria or exploring emerging rental hotspots where competition may be less intense. With average budgets showing modest annual growth, renters may find better value by considering slightly smaller properties or alternative locations within the capital.

item.title: Landlords need urgent clarity to hit 2030 rental energy targets, government warned
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government is facing calls to urgently clarify how private landlords can meet stricter energy efficiency targets by 2030, as industry experts warn that delayed guidance risks creating a last-minute rush to upgrade rental properties. A coalition of housing and energy organisations has demanded a clear roadmap for implementing new Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES), arguing that all parties need certainty to prepare effectively.

Industry calls for detailed implementation plan

A recent parliamentary roundtable, chaired by Clive Betts MP and attended by 12 key organisations, revealed widespread support for the government's Warm Homes Plan but highlighted significant concerns about the lack of detailed guidance. Participants including the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) and Energy Saving Trust warned that without clarity on exemptions, enforcement and financial support, many landlords might postpone improvements until closer to the deadline.

Ben Beadle of the NRLA commented: "Whilst the proposed framework has become more workable following recent government announcements, the focus must now shift to practical delivery. Upgrading properties on this scale requires landlords, contractors, local authorities and tenants to begin preparing immediately – 2030 may seem distant, but the scale of work required is substantial."

Key challenges facing the sector

The report identifies two major barriers to meeting the 2030 targets. Firstly, many landlords may struggle to access suitable financing options for energy efficiency improvements. Secondly, the UK currently faces a shortage of qualified installers capable of delivering retrofit work at the required volume.

  • Financial institutions need clearer guidelines to develop appropriate landlord finance products
  • The retrofit industry requires certainty to justify investment in training programmes
  • Local authorities need resources to effectively enforce the new standards

Industry leaders suggest that delayed action could create a bottleneck as 2030 approaches, potentially overwhelming supply chains and local enforcement teams. There are also concerns about quality control if work is rushed, emphasising the need for proper accreditation schemes.

With the private rental sector playing a crucial role in the UK's decarbonisation efforts, all parties appear to agree on the objectives – but are calling for detailed, practical guidance to make the targets achievable without unnecessary disruption to landlords or tenants.

A coalition of housing and energy organisations has demanded a clear roadmap for implementing new Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES), arguing that all parties need certainty to prepare effectively.

Industry calls for detailed implementation plan

A recent parliamentary roundtable, chaired by Clive Betts MP and attended by 12 key organisations, revealed widespread support for the government's Warm Homes Plan but highlighted significant concerns about the lack of detailed guidance. Participants including the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) and Energy Saving Trust warned that without clarity on exemptions, enforcement and financial support, many landlords might postpone improvements until closer to the deadline.

The report identifies two major barriers to meeting the 2030 targets. Firstly, many landlords may struggle to access suitable financing options for energy efficiency improvements.   • The retrofit industry requires certainty to justify investment in training programmes
  • Local authorities need resources to effectively enforce the new standards

item.title: What Investors Should Prioritise When Refurbishing an Older Rental Property
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Older rental properties remain a popular choice among UK property investors, offering period charm, generous room proportions and often more competitive purchase prices than modern builds. However, these characterful homes can conceal costly issues behind their historic facades. For landlords considering refurbishing a period rental, strategic planning could help balance preservation with profitability.

Key Structural Considerations

Before focusing on cosmetic upgrades, landlords might prioritise assessing the fundamental integrity of an older property. Damp proofing often requires attention in Victorian or Edwardian homes, whilst roof conditions and structural timbers may need professional inspection. Addressing these issues early could prevent expensive emergency repairs later.

Electrical systems in period properties frequently require complete rewiring to meet modern safety standards, and plumbing may need updating to prevent leaks or low water pressure. Whilst preserving original features where possible, investors may wish to budget for these essential but less visible improvements before decorative work begins.

Balancing Character With Compliance

Period properties often boast attractive original features like fireplaces, cornices and sash windows. Where these elements remain in good condition, restoration rather than replacement could maintain the property's unique appeal whilst potentially increasing its rental value.

However, landlords must ensure all refurbishments comply with current regulations. Single-glazed windows may need secondary glazing to meet energy efficiency requirements, and original flooring might require treatment to eliminate trip hazards. The balance between preserving character and meeting legal standards could be crucial for both tenant satisfaction and regulatory compliance.

Modern Amenities For Competitive Rentals

Whilst maintaining historical charm, landlords might consider discreetly incorporating modern conveniences that today's tenants expect. Smart heating controls, USB charging points and high-speed broadband connections can make period properties more appealing without compromising their character.

Kitchens and bathrooms often benefit most from thoughtful modernisation. Fitting contemporary appliances within traditional cabinetry or choosing period-style sanitaryware could create attractive, functional spaces that command premium rents whilst respecting the property's heritage.

By approaching refurbishment methodically - addressing structural needs first, preserving character where possible and enhancing functionality - investors may transform older properties into desirable, compliant rentals that stand out in competitive markets.

item.title: Property industry puts housing supply at top of Labour conference wish list
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As Labour prepares for its annual conference in Liverpool, housing supply, support for first-time buyers, and rental reform have emerged as key priorities for the property industry. With an estimated 20,000 delegates and visitors expected to attend, the event marks Andy Burnham’s first conference as prime minister. Amid ongoing housing challenges, industry leaders are urging the government to address critical issues in the housing market, focusing on increasing supply and ensuring affordability for both buyers and renters.

Focus on Housing Supply and First-Time Buyers

Senior figures from LRG, a prominent property group, have outlined three key areas for action ahead of the conference. These include boosting housing supply, supporting first-time buyers, and making better use of England’s existing housing stock. Tim Foreman, managing director of Land and New Homes at LRG, emphasised that planning reform alone is insufficient to meet demand. He argued that developers need assurance that new homes will sell before committing to projects, particularly in the current economic climate.

Foreman highlighted the importance of first-time buyers in driving demand for new developments. He called for a targeted successor to the Help to Buy scheme, which supported over 387,000 property purchases between 2013 and 2023, with first-time buyers accounting for 328,000 of these. However, Foreman suggested that any new scheme should include regional price caps and income limits to ensure it benefits those who need it most.

Recent government figures underscore the scale of the housebuilding challenge. In 2025-26, England delivered an estimated 199,500 net additional homes, while new-build starts reached 130,170 in the year to March 2026. Foreman stressed that increasing supply requires not only planning permissions but also mechanisms to stimulate demand, particularly among first-time buyers.

Rental Reform and Supply Concerns

Alongside calls for increased housing supply, industry leaders are urging the government to consider the impact of recent reforms on the private rented sector. Allison Thompson, chief lettings officer at Leaders, highlighted the need to prioritise rental access and supply. She warned that restrictions on rent in advance could disadvantage tenants without conventional UK incomes, such as international students and those relocating to Britain.

Thompson also called for careful monitoring of rental reforms to ensure they do not inadvertently reduce supply or limit access for vulnerable groups. With demand for rental properties remaining high, she stressed the importance of balancing tenant protections with measures to support landlords and maintain a healthy rental market.

As Labour’s conference approaches, the property industry’s priorities reflect the ongoing challenges facing the UK housing market. Addressing these issues will require a coordinated approach, combining targeted support for first-time buyers, effective planning reforms, and balanced rental policies. With housing remaining a critical issue for the government, the outcomes of the conference could have significant implications for homeowners, renters, and the wider property market.

item.title: Think tank calls for stamp duty axe as Londoners ‘underpay’ £3.1bn in property tax
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A leading think tank has called for a radical shake-up of England's property taxation system, proposing the eventual abolition of stamp duty alongside council tax reforms. The Resolution Foundation's latest report suggests these changes could address regional imbalances and stimulate housing market activity.

The case for property tax reform

The current system, according to the think tank's analysis, creates significant distortions across England's housing market. Their research indicates London households effectively underpaid £3.1bn in property taxes during 2024-25 when comparing tax burdens to current property values. Meanwhile, homeowners in regions like the North East face disproportionate bills, with 85% expected to overpay by an average of £710 annually by 2030-31.

The Foundation highlights how council tax remains based on 1991 property valuations, despite dramatic regional variations in house price growth over three decades. This outdated system means many homeowners face tax bills that bear little relation to their property's current market value.

Proposed replacement system

The report advocates replacing both stamp duty and council tax with a single annual property tax calculated as 0.7% of a home's current value. This proportional system would aim to be revenue-neutral overall while addressing existing imbalances. Key features of the proposal include:

  • Protections for lower-income households through rebates
  • Payment deferral options for asset-rich but cash-poor homeowners
  • A transition period where stamp duty payments could offset future tax bills

The Foundation estimates stamp duty currently prevents around 100,000 property transactions annually, affecting everyone from downsizers to workers needing to relocate. However, they recommend maintaining the tax until wider reforms can be implemented, suggesting any changes should wait until after the current parliamentary term.

Regional impacts and next steps

The report highlights stark regional disparities in how the current system operates. While 80% of London households benefit from the existing structure, homeowners in other regions face growing imbalances. The Foundation suggests these inequalities will only widen without reform, particularly as property values continue to evolve at different rates across the country.

For homeowners considering their options, the proposals could signal potential future changes to property taxation. Whilst immediate reform seems unlikely, the research adds weight to growing calls for modernising England's property tax system to better reflect current housing market realities.

As the debate continues, borrowers and prospective movers may wish to stay informed about potential changes that could affect their long-term housing costs and mobility. The full impact of any reforms would likely vary significantly depending on property location and value.

item.title: Letting agents face strict new deadlines under damp and mould rules
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New regulations coming into force next month will impose strict deadlines on Scottish letting agents for addressing damp and mould issues in rental properties. The Investigation and Commencement of Repair (Scotland) Regulations 2026 take effect from 6 October 2026, introducing clear timelines for landlords to assess problems and initiate necessary repairs.

Key deadlines for damp and mould issues

Under the Scottish government guidelines, landlords will be required to:

  • Investigate reports of damp or mould within 10 working days
  • Provide tenants with a written summary of findings within 3 working days of completing the investigation
  • Commence any required repairs within 5 working days after the investigation concludes

These changes will necessitate significant operational adjustments for letting agents and property managers. Professionals in the sector may need to review their procedures for property inspections, contractor management, tenant communications and documentation practices. Some agencies might consider bringing in specialist damp and mould consultants to ensure compliance with the new rules.

Practical challenges for compliance

Propertymark has announced plans to host an information webinar to help agents prepare for the regulatory changes. The session will address several practical concerns, including:

  • Determining what constitutes a competent investigation
  • Handling cases where the cause of damp remains unclear
  • Managing situations where contractors cannot meet the repair deadlines

The regulations acknowledge that some circumstances may prevent strict adherence to timelines. In such cases, landlords must notify tenants about any delays and take reasonable steps to mitigate the impact. However, challenges may arise in rural areas where access to qualified contractors or specialists is limited.

Hazel MacIver, Policy and Campaigns Officer at Propertymark, commented: "While the regulations establish clear timescales, agents must also consider the practical aspects of implementation. This includes determining response protocols, identifying competent investigators, and maintaining comprehensive records."

Documentation and tenant responsibilities

The forthcoming webinar will also examine the critical role of record-keeping in demonstrating compliance. Agents and landlords will need to maintain detailed documentation showing how they've responded to each damp and mould report.

The session will additionally explore the relationship between landlords' obligations and tenant behaviours that might contribute to damp problems, such as inadequate heating, poor ventilation or moisture generation. This balanced approach recognises that maintaining property conditions often requires cooperation from both parties.

With the implementation date approaching, letting agents in Scotland would be wise to review their current processes and prepare for these significant changes to their operational requirements.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #455
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent housing reports highlight growing financial pressures for UK renters and landlords, with calls for policy changes and concerns over tenancy agreements. From frozen housing allowances to unsustainable rent-to-income ratios, the private rental sector faces mounting challenges.

Calls Grow to Unfreeze Local Housing Allowance

The Resolution Foundation has urged the government to restore the link between Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates and actual rental costs. Current data reveals over 1.1 million low-income households now face an average £100 monthly shortfall between LHA payments and local market rents. This gap could widen to 23.3% by October without intervention.

Stephen Hunsaker of the Resolution Foundation noted: "Many tenants receiving housing support already sacrifice essentials to cover rent. Restoring automatic annual adjustments to LHA could ease pressure on vulnerable renters in the private sector." The think tank recommends reintroducing automatic updates to reflect local rent changes in the upcoming budget.

Landlord Tenancy Agreement Concerns Emerge

A Lendlord survey reveals 90% of landlords don't have tenancy agreements legally reviewed, with only 25% trusting solicitors' wording when they do. Analysis of 5,235 agreements showed:

  • 79% now operate as periodic tenancies under the Renters' Rights Act
  • 5.7% use mixed fixed and rolling contracts
  • 14.5% retain fixed-term agreements only

Lendlord warned some landlords continue issuing ineffective fixed-term agreements, potentially facing £7,000 fines from local authorities. The platform emphasised landlords require clearer guidance on their obligations, noting 45% currently source agreements through letting agents rather than legal professionals.

Older Renters Face Affordability Crisis

Renters aged 70+ now spend 46% of their income on housing - significantly above the 40% threshold considered sustainable. Comparative figures show:

  • 20-29 year olds: 35% average
  • 60-69 year olds: 36% average

This disproportionate burden leaves older tenants struggling to cover other essential costs. With private rents continuing to rise, affordability challenges appear particularly acute for pension-aged renters lacking stable employment income.

These developments highlight systemic pressures across the rental market, from support mechanisms struggling to keep pace with inflation to legal compliance challenges for landlords. Both tenants and property owners may wish to stay informed as these issues develop.
